topics.content: The track languages differ in kind as well as in words. Kharadi, the speech of the orc holds, is terse and built around obligation. Veyran is a shared second language for peoples who each keep a tongue of their own at home. Iscaran is the working language of magic and of the portal network. Vesperan grew from a harbor trade speech and is the language of shipping and insurance. Starke, spoken in Hearthspire, is the least studied. Lowland, Breedhaven's own, has borrowed from all five.

question.ask: Which language is the working language of magic and of the portal network?

topics.title: Kharadi: The Grammar of a Given Word
topics.content: Kharadi marks on the verb whether a statement is a report or an undertaking. The plain form states a fact. The bound form, made with the suffix -akh, commits the speaker: it is a promise, the form used in contracts and by a War-Mother giving her word. Lowland has no such distinction, so the translator must supply it with shall, undertake or warrant, never with will, which reads as mere prediction. Mistaking a plain form for a bound one in a draft contract is the commonest serious error.

question.ask: What does the bound form of a Kharadi verb express?

topics.title: Veyran: Register and Indirection
topics.content: Assembly Veyran is nobody's mother tongue. It was standardized so that delegates of many peoples could legislate together, and it shows: regular grammar, few idioms, and an elaborate system of softening. A flat refusal is almost never written. A sentence saying it is conceivable that the committee will return to this means no. Rendered word for word into Lowland it gives a false impression of agreement. The practice is to translate the force of the sentence and footnote the form.

question.ask: What is the practice for translating a softened Assembly Veyran sentence?
question.answer: Translate the force, footnote the form
wrong: Translate the form, footnote the force

topics.title: Iscaran Magical Terminology
topics.content: Lowland took most of its technical vocabulary of magic from Iscaran, and the borrowings have drifted. Iscaran distinguishes a working done once by hand from a working fixed in an object; Lowland says enchantment loosely for both. Iscaran tier terms name the number of casters required, where Breedhaven tiers grade output and hazard, so the two scales do not map one to one. The rule for technical translation is to keep the source term at first use, gloss it, and never substitute a near equivalent.

question.ask: What do Iscaran tier terms name?

topics.title: Vesperan and Starke: Contract and Measure
topics.content: Vesperan legal prose descends from ship's articles, and its key terms are shares. A party does not own a venture; she holds a lay in it, and a lay carries a matching portion of loss as well as gain. Rendering lay as stake or interest drops the liability. Starke poses the opposite problem, a word with too much in it: hearthmark is both a currency and a measured share of warmth, so a Starke price is literally a quantity of heat. Translators leave it untranslated and gloss it once.

question.ask: In Vesperan legal prose, what does a party hold in a venture?

topics.title: Equivalence, Untranslatables and Back-Translation
topics.content: Two aims pull against each other: formal equivalence, which keeps the wording, and functional equivalence, which keeps the effect. Legal and magical texts lean formal, because a court or a caster will act on the words. Kinship terms resist both. A Kharadi hold is not a Lowland household, and Second Bloom has no neat equivalent abroad. The working check is back-translation: a second translator returns the draft to the source language, and every mismatch is examined.

question.ask: Which check has a second translator return the draft to the source language?

skill.name: The right first words
skill.description: You know how to open with anyone: affection from your first scene with a woman is doubled.

courses.title: Foundations of Child Care
courses.description: How infants and young children are raised in Breedhaven: the creche and the household nursery, a child's first months, and the work of the nannies and teachers who do most of it. Includes placement hours at the University creche.

topics.title: Who Raises a Child
topics.content: In Breedhaven a child is rarely raised by two people. The usual household has several adults, and the law names each mother's own children as hers while leaving the daily work to whoever is home. Where a household cannot manage, the creche can: every district keeps one, and the University's takes a student's child from the first week at no charge. A third arrangement is the nanny, employed by the household or, for a registered Sire, by the Office. The course treats all three as ordinary.

question.ask: What does every district keep for households that cannot manage a child's care?

topics.title: The First Six Weeks
topics.content: A newborn's needs in the first six weeks are few and constant: feeding every two to three hours, warmth, sleep and being held. Crying is its only signal and has a small number of causes, checked in order: hunger, a wet cloth, wind, cold, tiredness. A child that is fed, clean, warm and still crying usually wants to be carried. Weight is taken weekly and should climb steadily after the first few days. A carer who keeps a simple written record sees a problem days before one who trusts memory.

question.ask: What does a baby that is fed, clean, warm and still crying usually want?

topics.title: Sleep, and Where a Child Sleeps
topics.content: An infant sleeps most of the day in short stretches, and where it sleeps matters. A cot of its own, on its back, with nothing loose in it, is the standard taught in every clinic. The room is kept cool and free of draughts. A listening charm on the sill is common in houses with a nursery and carries a cry to whoever wears its twin. Children settle faster on a fixed routine: the same order of bath, feed and song each evening does more than any working sold for the purpose.

question.ask: In what position is an infant put to sleep in its cot?

topics.title: Seven Daughters and a Son
topics.content: Seven children in eight are girls, and nurseries are built around that. Girls show their first unreliable magic between five and seven, and a creche for that age is warded, with soft floors and nothing breakable above waist height. Boys are few, noticed, and too often either indulged or fussed over. Good practice treats a son like any other child in the room and resists making him a mascot. Whether a boy will be fertile cannot be known before he is grown, and carers are taught not to guess aloud.

question.ask: At what ages do girls show their first unreliable magic?

topics.title: What a Child Costs
topics.content: Keeping a child at home has a weekly cost that students of the subject learn to itemize: milk or a wet nurse's fee, cloths, clothes outgrown in weeks, fuel for a warm room and the carer's time. A household that skimps shows it first in the child, who grows fretful and slow to gain. One that spends steadily sees a child settle and then thrive. Comfort in the house sets the ceiling: a dedicated nursery, a garden and a calm household let a child do better than money alone can buy.

question.ask: What sets the ceiling on how well a child can do at home?

topics.title: The Carer and the Parents
topics.content: A nanny or creche worker serves the child first and the household second, and trouble comes when the two pull apart. The working rules are plain. She reports what she sees, good and bad, without softening. She does not take sides between a child's mother and the other adults of the house. She keeps what she learns of the family to herself. And she says early when a child is not being provided for, because a carer who stays silent to keep her post has stopped doing the job.

question.ask: Whom does a nanny or creche worker serve first?

skill.name: Good with children
skill.description: Children in your house can come to do one level better.

courses.title: Media, Image and the Public Eye
courses.description: How reputation is made and lost in a country that lives on its phones: Bloomr and the feed, the press, the public life of a Sire, and the difference between being known and being talked about.

topics.title: How a Feed Decides
topics.content: Bloomr shows a post to a few of the poster's followers first and then widens or buries it by how they respond in the opening hour. Likes count for little; replies and shares count for much more. A picture with a face in it travels further than one without. The practical lesson is timing and reply: a post made when followers are awake, and answered by its author in the first hour, reaches several times the audience of the same post left alone. Nothing about the feed is neutral, and nothing about it is secret.

question.ask: On Bloomr, which responses count for much more than likes?

topics.title: Reputation Is What Others Repeat
topics.content: A reputation is not what a person says of herself but what a third party will repeat about her unprompted. It is built by small consistent acts seen by others: turning up, remembering a name, keeping a confidence. It travels through people, so one well-connected friend who speaks warmly is worth a hundred posts. It is also sticky in both directions. A good name survives one bad evening, and a bad one is not repaired by a single generous gesture, however public.

question.ask: What builds a reputation?
question.answer: Small consistent acts seen by others

topics.title: The Public Life of a Sire
topics.content: A registered Sire is a public figure whether he chooses to be or not. His Registry record is private by law, but where he was seen and with whom is not, and the gossip press pays for both. Coverage follows a pattern: curiosity when he is new, scrutiny when he is linked with several women, and judgment when a child is born. Sires who fare well are seen keeping their word and are never seen boasting. The public forgives a full household far more readily than a careless one.

question.ask: What about a registered Sire is private by law?

topics.title: Gossip, and How It Moves
topics.content: Gossip moves fastest between people who share a room: a seminar, a hall, a shift. It is passed on because telling it buys standing, so the most repeated stories flatter the teller's judgment. A rumor denied loudly spreads further than one ignored, and one corrected quietly by a trusted friend tends to die. On a campus of thirty thousand, a story about a known figure crosses it in about two days. The useful habit is to assume that anything done before two witnesses will be known by all three households.

question.ask: How long does a story about a known figure take to cross the campus?

topics.title: Writing a Message That Lands
topics.content: A message is read in the first eight words or not at all. The working rules are short: say the one thing, say it early, and end on something the reader can answer. Warmth survives in writing only when it is specific, so naming the thing remembered does more than any endearment. A reply sent within the hour reads as interest; the same reply a day late reads as duty. Humor travels badly without a face behind it, which is why a careless joke starts more quarrels by text than in person.

question.ask: How does a reply sent a day late read to the person receiving it?

topics.title: Handling a Bad Story
topics.content: When a damaging story breaks, the first hour decides its shape. The steps are fixed. Find out what is true before saying anything. If it is true, say so once, plainly, and say what will be done. If it is false, have someone else correct it, because a denial from the subject is discounted. Never answer in anger and never answer every critic. Then be seen doing something ordinary and decent. Most stories last four days, and the person who feeds one makes it last twelve.

question.ask: If a damaging story is false, who should correct it?

skill.name: A good name
skill.description: You are spoken well of: every woman needs 5 less desire.

courses.title: Household Enchantment and Management
courses.description: Practical and theoretical introduction to the enchanted household: built-in wards, preservation charms, heating and lighting systems, garden magic, and the domestic economy of a magitech home. No prerequisites.

topics.title: The Household as an Institution
topics.content: The ordinary family of Breedhaven is a household: several adults who share a home, money and the raising of children. A common shape is one Sire and two to five women, but households of women alone are just as usual. Most set down a house agreement when they form, a plain written list of who the members are, what each pays into the common purse, who owns which furniture, and how a member joins or leaves. It is not romantic, and households that write one last longer than those that do not.

question.ask: What written document do most households set down when they form?

topics.title: Wards on Doors and Windows
topics.content: A threshold ward is set into the door frame when a house is built and keyed to the people who live there. It does not stop a determined burglar; it wakes the household and marks the intruder. Wards weaken with use and are renewed once a season, a ten-minute job for any woman in the house. Keying a new member to the door is done with everyone present, as a small courtesy with real weight. Rooms kept for a pregnant member are given a second, inward ward, to protect the plaster from her.

question.ask: How often are a house's threshold wards renewed?

topics.title: Preservation Charms and the Larder
topics.content: A preservation charm slows spoilage by holding a cupboard or larder at about four degrees and still air. A well-cast one lasts a week and fades from the door inward, so the food nearest the hinge spoils first. Most homes keep both a charmed larder and an electric refrigerator: the larder for bread, fruit, cheese and anything eaten within days, the refrigerator for meat and milk. Renewing the charm goes on the house rota like any other chore, with the date chalked on the inside of the door.

question.ask: In a home with both, where are meat and milk kept?

topics.title: Heat, Light and the Monthly Bills
topics.content: A warming charm heats one room for an evening and costs nothing but effort; a boiler heats the whole house and costs money. Sensible homes use the boiler as a base and charms to top up. Costs are met from a common purse, usually paid into in proportion to income. A worked example: five adults each pay in three tenths of what they earn, so a member earning 2,000 a month gives 600 and one earning 1,000 gives 300. Rent, heat, light and food come out of the purse; the rest stays private.

question.ask: How do members usually pay into a household's common purse?

topics.title: Garden Magic and the Kitchen Plot
topics.content: Coaxing plants is among the commonest magics, and nearly every household keeps a plot or at least a window box. A growth charm brings a crop on about a third faster, but the plant draws the difference from the soil, so charmed beds need compost dug in twice a year. A four-bed rotation moves roots, greens, beans and fruiting crops round one place each spring. Fruit trees are coaxed lightly and only at blossom. Over-charmed tomatoes are the classic beginner's error: large, watery and tasteless.

question.ask: How much faster does a growth charm bring a crop on?

topics.title: The House Meeting and Its Manners
topics.content: A household that works keeps a weekly meeting, short and at the kitchen table. Three things are settled: the rota for cooking, cleaning and children, the state of the purse, and anything that needs saying. Etiquette is exact on the last point. Who is with whom is said plainly, and a member who wants a new partner raises it with the house first. Wanting is no offense; going behind the household's back is. Jealousy is treated as ordinary weather, to be named early and not left to sour.

question.ask: What should a household member who wants a new partner do first?

skill.name: An eye for taste
skill.description: After time spent with a woman you work out one thing she likes or dislikes that you did not know.

courses.title: Psychology of the Bloom
courses.description: Introduction to the psychological dimensions of the Bloom in women: the generative drive, its developmental trajectory, its intensification in pregnancy, and its absence after menopause. Covers damper effects and the psychology of Sire proximity. No prerequisites.

topics.title: The Generative Drive
topics.content: In women the Bloom is felt as a drive toward generativity: to create, nurture, grow and protect life. Bearing a child is its strongest expression, but not its only one. The same drive is at work in the gardener, the teacher, the healer and the woman who guards a door. Bloom Psychology treats it as an instinct like hunger: it supplies wanting and never decides action. A person can be hungry and decline a meal, and the same holds here.

question.ask: Bloom Psychology treats the generative drive as an instinct like what?

topics.title: From Adolescence to Adulthood
topics.content: The drive is faint in childhood and rises through adolescence alongside a girl's first reliable magic. It is strongest in young adults and in women who have never carried a child, and usually settles after a first pregnancy into something steadier. University age is close to the peak, which is one reason Bloom Counseling is free on campus. Strength varies widely between individuals, and a weak drive and a strong one are equally normal.

question.ask: After what event does the drive usually settle into something steadier?

topics.title: Proximity to a Sire
topics.content: Near a Sire a woman feels the pull as warmth, heightened attention and want. It arises in the body before any thought and does not wait for her to know his status, which is one way that status leaks. The classic finding is attention drift: asked to read aloud in a shared room, subjects glance toward a Sire several times more often than toward other men, and underestimate how often they did so. The pull is a feeling. What follows it is a choice.

question.ask: What is the finding that women glance more often toward a Sire called?

topics.title: Dampers and the Background Hum
topics.content: Bloom suppressants, called dampers, are cheap, legal and ordinary. Taken daily, they turn the pull down to what users describe as a background hum: present and ignorable, like traffic behind a closed window. They do not dull magic, mood or affection. Common reasons for use are study, work near Sires and simply wanting quiet. Stopping brings the pull back to full strength within days, and the first week off is often reported as louder than remembered.

question.ask: How often are dampers taken?

topics.title: The Pregnant Mind
topics.content: Pregnancy is the drive's strongest pull and its strongest expression at once. Protectiveness rises sharply, attention narrows toward home and household, and many women report a settled confidence that accompanies the surge in power. A mother often feels the child's moods as her own and senses other pregnancies nearby. The psychological risk is overreach: strength arrives in weeks, faster than judgment can adjust to it. After the birth, mood and power fall together.

question.ask: What is the main psychological risk of pregnancy?

topics.title: Second Bloom and Whose Want
topics.content: After menopause the pull is absent. Women in these years, called the Second Bloom, commonly describe relief, clarity and time that is their own, and some describe loss. Their testimony feeds the oldest argument. Bloomists hold that the Bloom's wants are sacred and truly a woman's own. Freewill advocates answer that the Bloom may influence a woman but does not own her. Psychology cannot settle it, but can show that a want felt as one's own may still have an outside cause.

question.ask: What are a woman's years after menopause called?

skill.name: Reading desire
skill.description: You can tell how much a woman would have to want you before she would go to bed with you: her profile says how far there is to go.

courses.title: Introduction to Computing
courses.description: Fundamentals of programming, data structures, and algorithms, with applications to enchantment modeling, ward simulation, and Registry database systems. Weekly laboratory covers hands-on coding and debugging. No prerequisites.

topics.title: Algorithms: Instructions Without Judgment
topics.content: An algorithm is a finite list of exact steps that turns an input into an output. A computer follows it with no judgment: unlike a working, which varies with the woman casting and how tired she is, a program gives the same answer every time. Programs keep values in named variables with types: an integer for a tram number, a decimal for a ward's charge, a string for a Bloomr handle, a boolean for whether a door is locked. First exercise: compute the hours until a lamp charm needs renewing.

question.ask: Which variable type records whether a door is locked?

topics.title: Branches, Loops and Functions
topics.content: Three structures build every program. A branch chooses: if the ward's charge is below threshold, raise an alert, otherwise do nothing. A loop repeats: for each of the forty doors in a residence hall, read its ward and record the value. A function names a piece of work so it can be reused: charge_remaining(initial, half_life, days) returns a number and hides the arithmetic. Most loop bugs are off-by-one errors; checking thirty-nine doors out of forty is the classic.

question.ask: Which program structure repeats a step for each of forty doors?

topics.title: Lists, Dictionaries and Queues
topics.content: A data structure arranges values so the common operation is fast. A list keeps items in order and is read by position: the stops on a tram line. A dictionary maps a key to a value and finds it in one step however large it grows: a handle to an account. A queue serves first come, first served: travelers waiting at a teleport array, which sends one group at a time. Finding one account among thirty thousand in an unsorted list takes fifteen thousand comparisons on average; a dictionary takes one.

question.ask: How many steps does a dictionary take to find one account?

topics.title: Searching, Sorting and Cost
topics.content: Cost is counted in steps as the input grows. Linear search checks every record: a million records, up to a million steps. Binary search works on sorted data, halving the range each time: a million records in at most twenty steps, since two to the twentieth exceeds a million. Merge sort splits a list in half, sorts each half and merges them, taking about n log n steps: twenty million for a million records, against a trillion for the naive method of comparing every pair.

question.ask: What must be true of the data before binary search can be used?
wrong: It must be in a queue

topics.title: Databases and the Sire Registry
topics.content: A database stores records in tables, each row found by a unique key. The national Sire Registry is a system designed around who may read it. Each assay record is held under a reference number, not a name; the table linking numbers to people is kept apart and encrypted. The record is private by law, so access is by role, a clinician sees only her own patients, and every query is written to a log that cannot be edited. Sound design assumes leaks come from people with access, not from broken code.

question.ask: Under what is each assay record in the Sire Registry held?

topics.title: Simulating Wards in Software
topics.content: A model is a program that imitates a real system well enough to answer a question. A ward can be modeled as a state machine with three states, armed, tripped and drained, and rules for moving between them. A simulation steps time forward, one hour per loop, reducing the charge by its decay rate and testing the threshold. Run for a year, it predicts the service date before any stone is charged. A model is only as good as its measurements: a wrong half-life gives a confident wrong answer.

question.ask: Which three states does a ward modeled as a state machine have?

skill.name: Pattern of life
skill.description: You can work out where a woman usually is through the week: her profile lists it.

courses.title: Calculus and Statistics
courses.description: Differential and integral calculus with an introduction to probability and statistics, emphasizing applications in magical engineering, thaumic measurement, and biological assay. No prerequisites.

topics.title: Rates of Change and the Derivative
topics.content: The derivative measures how fast one quantity changes with another: the slope of its graph at a point. If a ward holds Q(t) thaums at time t, then dQ/dt is its rate of loss. By the power rule, the derivative of t squared is 2t, of t cubed is 3t squared. Worked example: a pregnant mage's output is modeled as P(t) = 40 + 5t squared thaums per hour, with t in weeks. Then dP/dt = 10t, so at week six her output is rising by 60 thaums per hour each week, twice the rate at week three.

question.ask: By the power rule, what is the derivative of t squared?

topics.title: Integration and Accumulated Charge
topics.content: Integration reverses differentiation and measures accumulation: the area under a curve. If r(t) is the rate at which a circle pours charge into an anchor, the integral of r from start to finish is the total charge delivered. Worked example: a circle charges a station array at r(t) = 60t squared thaums per hour for two hours. The total is 20t cubed evaluated from 0 to 2, which is 160 thaums. The fundamental theorem of calculus states that the two operations undo each other.

question.ask: What does integration measure on a graph?

topics.title: Exponential Decay and Half-Life
topics.content: A quantity that loses a fixed fraction of itself per unit time decays exponentially: Q(t) = Q0 times e to the power minus kt. It solves dQ/dt = minus kQ. The half-life is ln 2 divided by k, about 0.693 over k. Worked example: a household ward plate has a half-life of six months and fails below a quarter of full charge. A quarter is two halvings, so it lasts twelve months and must be serviced before then. The same curve describes cooling, drug clearance and assay reagents.

question.ask: When does a ward plate with a six-month half-life fall to a quarter of full charge?

topics.title: Probability and the Seven-to-One Ratio
topics.content: Probability assigns each outcome a number from 0 to 1. Seven girls are born for every boy, so the chance that a birth is a boy is 1 in 8, or 0.125. About one man in ten is a Sire, and independent chances multiply: 1/8 times 1/10 gives 1 birth in 80. Worked example: a mother of three. The chance all three are daughters is 7/8 cubed, about 0.67, so the chance of at least one son is 0.33. The complement rule, one minus the chance of none, is the quickest route to any at-least-one question.

question.ask: What is the chance that a birth is a boy?

topics.title: Expected Counts and the Binomial Distribution
topics.content: When n independent trials each succeed with chance p, the number of successes is binomial, with mean np and standard deviation the square root of np(1 minus p). Worked example: a hall of 200 drawn at random from a population that is one-eighth male. Expected men: 25. Standard deviation: the root of 200 times 1/8 times 7/8, about 4.7, so 16 to 34 men covers nearly every such hall. Expected Sires at 1 in 80: 2.5, and the chance of none at all is 79/80 to the power 200, about 8 percent.

question.ask: What is the mean of a binomial count with n trials and chance p?

topics.title: Conditional Probability and Assay Error
topics.content: The inverse probability rule turns the chance of a result given a condition into the chance of the condition given the result. Suppose a screening assay detects 99 percent of fertile men and wrongly flags 2 percent of infertile ones. Of 1,000 men tested, 100 are fertile and 99 test positive; 900 are not and 18 test positive. So 99 of 117 positives are true, about 85 percent: nearly one positive in six is false. Hence the case for confirming any positive with a second assay.

question.ask: In the screening assay example, about what share of positive results are false?

skill.name: Working it through
skill.description: You study efficiently: study and Focus earn a quarter more marks.

courses.title: Prenatal Thaumaturgy
courses.description: Survey of the magical changes of pregnancy and their practical applications and risks. Weekly laboratory covers measurement of gestational thaumic output, prenatal warding, and safety protocols for pregnant practitioners. No prerequisites.

topics.title: The Gestational Curve
topics.content: A woman's thaumic output rises through pregnancy along a known curve. In the early weeks the lift is slight, about a fifth above her baseline. By the middle of term it has doubled or trebled. Near term it commonly reaches eight to ten times baseline, so that a middling caster can exceed a trained professor. The curve is plotted against her own resting figure and never against other women, because baselines differ far more than the multipliers do.

question.ask: Near term, how high does a woman's thaumic output commonly reach?

topics.title: Measuring Gestational Output
topics.content: Output is measured weekly with a thaumometer at the wrist, seated, after ten minutes of rest and before any casting that day. The reading is entered on a gestational chart beside the baseline taken at registration. A jump of more than half in a single week is reported to the clinic. Readings are unreliable for an hour after strong emotion, and whenever another pregnant woman is within a few meters, since fields that near raise one another.

question.ask: Where on the body is the weekly thaumometer reading taken?

topics.title: Hardiness and the Sympathetic Sense
topics.content: Pregnancy changes more than output. The mother becomes hardier: she heals faster, tires later and resists cold and minor illness. She senses other pregnancies nearby, usually as a warmth with a direction to it, sometimes before the other woman has told anyone. And she commonly feels the child's moods as her own, a restlessness or a calm with no cause in her own day. Practitioners are taught to ask of any sudden feeling whether it is truly theirs.

question.ask: How does a pregnant woman usually sense another pregnancy nearby?
question.answer: As a warmth with a direction
wrong: As a ringing in the ears

topics.title: Prenatal Warding and Field Leakage
topics.content: A surging field leaks, and leaks do damage: cracked plaster, blown bulbs, soured milk, a kettle boiled dry. Prenatal warding contains it. A personal ward, worn as a band or stitched into a hem, bleeds excess power into the ground. Room wards are set into walls and floor, which is why pregnant students are offered ground-floor rooms. Wards are rated in thaums and must be re-rated as term advances, since a ward fitted early will be overwhelmed later.

question.ask: Where does a personal prenatal ward bleed excess power?

topics.title: Protocols for the Pregnant Practitioner
topics.content: Practical classes are streamed by tier, and pregnancy overturns the streaming. A woman who could not hold a Tier III working may exceed it by the middle of her term, so she is moved into advanced practicals while the surge lasts. Three rules apply there. She works at a warded bench. A spotter stands ready to ground the working. And she casts at half effort first, because the habit of pushing hard, learned when she was weaker, is what wrecks laboratories.

question.ask: At what effort must a pregnant practitioner cast first in advanced practicals?

topics.title: Birth Discharge and the Bloom Chamber
topics.content: Birth ends the surge at a stroke. The stored field leaves the mother in a single discharge strong enough to crack masonry, and within hours her output falls to near baseline. Hospitals therefore deliver in Bloom Chambers: rooms with layered wards in walls, floor and ceiling that carry the discharge safely to ground. Midwives work inside under personal wards. The discharge harms neither mother nor child, only whatever stands unwarded nearby.

question.ask: In what kind of room do hospitals deliver babies?

skill.name: Ward reading
skill.description: You can tell whether a woman is taking anything against the Bloom: her profile says whether she is on birth control.

courses.title: Reproductive Biology of the Sown Expanse
courses.description: The biology of the seven-to-one sex ratio, Sire fertility, and the mechanisms by which pregnancy amplifies a woman's magic. Weekly laboratory introduces assay techniques, basic histology, and statistical analysis of fertility data. No prerequisites.

topics.title: Seven Daughters to a Son
topics.content: In every nation and every people of the Sown Expanse, seven girls are born for each boy. A hall of two hundred therefore holds about twenty-five men. Because only one man in ten is fertile, a town of eight thousand people contains about a thousand men and about a hundred Sires. The ratio is fixed at conception and not by losses in the womb: miscarriage rates are the same for daughters and sons. Everything else in reproductive biology follows from these figures.

question.ask: How many girls are born for each boy in the Sown Expanse?

topics.title: Fertile and Infertile Seed
topics.content: All men produce seed, and under an ordinary microscope a Sire's sample looks like any other. The difference appears with a Bloom-reactive stain. Bound seed carries a trace of the Bloom and can enter an egg. Unbound seed swims normally and is turned away at the egg's surface. A Sire's sample contains a substantial share of bound seed, and other men's almost none. The standard laboratory exercise is to count the bound cells among two hundred on a prepared slide.

question.ask: What shows the difference between a Sire's seed and other men's?

topics.title: Conception and the Lock-In
topics.content: Conception needs bound seed, a ripe egg and a body not under contraception. When all three meet, the mother's field closes around the new life within moments. This is the lock-in, and most women report feeling it at once as certainty and a rush of magic. Daily suppressants, long-acting implants and ward-charms all work by keeping the field from closing, so that no pregnancy begins. A healer can set a ward-charm in a minute, and all three are free at any clinic.

question.ask: What is the closing of the mother's field around a new life called?

topics.title: The Hurried Term
topics.content: The Bloom hastens pregnancy. A term is counted in weeks, and under two months from conception to birth is ordinary. Growth that would otherwise take far longer is driven by the mother's field, which feeds the child directly alongside the placenta. The cost is appetite and rest: a pregnant woman may eat half as much again and sleep ten hours a night. Clinics see patients weekly, since a single week of such a pregnancy covers a great deal of development.

question.ask: How long is an ordinary pregnancy from conception to birth?

topics.title: Why Pregnancy Amplifies Magic
topics.content: A pregnant woman's power rises from the first weeks: a small lift early, a marked one in the middle of term and exceptional strength near the end. Two mechanisms are accepted. The child has a field of its own, which adds to the mother's. And the placenta acts as a Bloom organ, gathering and concentrating the field as it gathers nutrients. The child of a high-assay Sire tends to produce a stronger surge, a difference of degree and not of kind.

question.ask: Which organ gathers and concentrates the Bloom's field during pregnancy?

topics.title: Reading Fertility Data
topics.content: A worked example. The University has about thirty thousand students, one in eight of them men: 3,750. One in ten of those is expected to be fertile: about 375. Suppose a hall of 400 residents were found to hold twelve Sires where five are expected. Is that chance? Small counts swing widely, yet the test shows a result this high would arise by luck less than one time in a hundred. The habit to learn is stating the expected figure before looking at the observed one.

question.ask: What should be stated before looking at an observed figure?

skill.name: Cycle sense
skill.description: You can tell when a woman is on her period: her profile says so.

courses.title: Studio Art Foundations
courses.description: Introduction to drawing, painting, and sculptural practice, with attention to the use of Bloom-infused pigments and materials. Weekly laboratory provides guided studio time and critique. No prerequisites.

topics.title: Line, Contour and Learning to See
topics.content: Drawing starts with the eye, not the hand. A contour drawing follows the edge of a form slowly, without lifting the charcoal; a gesture drawing catches the whole pose in thirty seconds. Proportion is checked by sighting: a pencil held at arm's length, the thumb marking the height of a head, then counted down the figure, which stands about seven and a half heads tall. By long studio tradition the first term is worked unaided, with no steadying charm on the hand, so the skill is truly learned.

question.ask: About how many heads tall does the human figure stand?

topics.title: Value, Light and Form
topics.content: Value is how light or dark a tone is, set out on a scale of nine steps from white paper to the blackest charcoal. A lit sphere shows five zones: highlight, halftone, core shadow, reflected light and cast shadow. Rendering those five turns a flat circle into a ball. Enchanted lighting is soft and comes from every side, which flattens form, so studios are built with tall north windows and life drawing is done by daylight or by a single plain lamp set high and to one side of the model.

question.ask: Which way do the tall windows of a drawing studio face?

topics.title: Color and Bloom-Infused Pigments
topics.content: The three primaries are red, yellow and blue; mixing two gives a secondary, and colors opposite on the wheel dull each other toward gray. Bloom-infused pigments are ground from minerals and plants taken from Bloom-rich ground and bound in oil or egg. They are not illusions but living color: orchard green, made from moss, deepens over decades, and some reds warm visibly in a crowded room. They are costly and fade in direct sun, so a painter uses them for accents and plain pigment for the rest.

question.ask: Why do painters keep Bloom-infused pigments for accents only?
question.answer: They are costly and fade in sunlight
wrong: They are illusions that vanish in days
They are poisonous to handle for long
They are reserved by law for the Order

topics.title: Painting Traditions of Breedhaven
topics.content: Two genres define Breedhaven painting. The first is the orchard landscape: low horizons, rivers, trees in blossom, painted outdoors in a single sitting. The second is the household portrait, the national form for some three centuries. Its convention is that the adults of a house are shown in a ring or a loose group at one table, none set above the others, with the children in front. Court portraits of House Dawnbloom follow an older rule: the queen stands alone, holding a flowering branch.

question.ask: Which genre has been Breedhaven's national form of painting for three centuries?

topics.title: Art of the Neighboring Nations
topics.content: Each neighbor has a signature craft. Kharad-Tor works steel: chased relief panels and the woven banners that hang in every hold. Veyra carves theater masks, and a mask-maker ranks there with a painter. The Vesperan League prizes painted sea charts and ship figureheads. Iscara has ward-calligraphy, where the written working is itself the ornament. In the Starkelands, sculptors in Hearthspire work glass and ice lit from within, an art made for a city that spends half the year in the dark.

question.ask: Which nation's signature craft is the carved theater mask?

topics.title: Clay, Stone and Sculptural Form
topics.content: Sculpture is either additive, built up in clay or wax over a wire armature, or subtractive, cut away from wood or stone. Clay shrinks by about a tenth as it dries and fires, so work is modeled oversize, and walls thicker than a thumb are hollowed or they burst in the kiln. A mending charm must never be used on a crack in wet clay: it seals the surface and traps the flaw. Self-mending building stone closes over every chisel cut, so carvers order plain quarry stone that has never been warded.

question.ask: About how much does clay shrink as it dries and fires?

skill.name: A steady hand
skill.description: Work on dexterity goes half as far again.

courses.title: Peoples and Politics of the Sown Expanse
courses.description: Comparative survey of the nations and peoples of the Sown Expanse: their governments, economies, magical traditions, and relations with Breedhaven. Covers the regions beyond the Expanse and the status of migrants and outsiders. No prerequisites.

topics.title: The Shape of the Sown Expanse
topics.content: The Sown Expanse is the known world, and the Bloom reaches all of it. In every nation seven girls are born for each boy, magic belongs to women, and about one man in ten is fertile. Six states matter most. Breedhaven is a green lowland kingdom of rivers and orchards. North lies Kharad-Tor, east Veyra, with Iscara, the Vesperan League and the Starkelands beyond. Rail, shipping, the net and a few long-range portal lines join them, and a Sire of record assay is news in all six.

question.ask: How many states of the Sown Expanse matter most?

topics.title: Kharad-Tor and the Holds
topics.content: Kharad-Tor is the orc federation of the red hills north of Breedhaven. Its wealth is mines, steelworks and mountain rail, and its army is the most disciplined in the Expanse. The basic unit is the hold, a large extended household led by a War-Mother who has proved she can protect her people and keep her word. The Council of War-Mothers governs. Kharadi are blunt, loyal and exact about contracts, and they bargain openly for lawful access to strong Sires for their holds.

question.ask: What is the leader of a Kharadi hold called?

topics.title: Veyra, Federation of the Beastkin
topics.content: Veyra lies east of Breedhaven and is shared by foxkin, catkin, wolfkin, rabbitkin and many smaller peoples under an elected National Assembly. No people holds a majority, so every government is a coalition and compromise is the national skill. Its diplomats are accordingly very good. Veyra also runs the Quiet Office, the most capable intelligence service in the Expanse, whose emblem is two masks, one smiling and one blank. Veyrans abroad are often, and unfairly, suspected of reporting to it.

question.ask: Why is every government of Veyra a coalition?

topics.title: Iscara, the State of Mages
topics.content: Iscara is governed by its mages, and office is earned by demonstrated ability. The head of state, the Sorceress Queen, wins her title in open demonstration. Iscaran magic is the best organized anywhere: the state built and runs the long-range portal network, its wards protect half the world's ports, and its disaster teams are the ones other nations call. Since pregnancy multiplies power, its greatest workings are led by pregnant mages, and it takes a frank, clinical interest in strong Sires.

question.ask: How does Iscara's Sorceress Queen win her title?

topics.title: The Vesperan League and the Starkelands
topics.content: The Vesperan League is islands and harbor cities, founded by pirate queens who agreed to divide the sea lanes instead of raiding each other. It lives by shipping, insurance and banking, and its elected High Queen governs from the Admiralty Exchange. The Starkelands are the frozen north, where humans and dark elves live almost entirely in one enclosed city, Hearthspire, on geothermal heat. The Council of Hearths governs, and the hearthmark, its currency, is a measured share of warmth.

question.ask: In which enclosed city do nearly all Starkelanders live?

topics.title: Peoples, Migrants and Outsiders
topics.content: Humans are Breedhaven's majority, yet the country is not thought of as human. Elves are common in the old families and the Order, halflings in the cities, and foxkin from Veyra are long settled. Orcs from Kharad-Tor work in every trade, most visibly the army and the building sites. Slimes keep to the water and hold full personhood. Since the Expanse is the whole known world, an outsider means a foreign national, and what lies past the charted seas and the northern ice is unsurveyed.

question.ask: Which people make up Breedhaven's majority?

skill.name: Knowing what travels
skill.description: You know where a thing is from and why it matters: a gift that lands is worth half as much again.

courses.title: The Bloom in History
courses.description: A general-education survey of the Primordial Bloom as a historical force, from oral traditions and early natural philosophy to its role in the founding of the Sown Expanse's modern states. No prerequisites.

topics.title: Before Writing: The Oral Tradition
topics.content: The oldest knowledge of the Bloom was carried in sayings, songs and counting rhymes long before anyone wrote it down. Every people of the Expanse has a version of the seven petals rhyme, counting seven daughters before a son, and the Seven Petals shop sign is its last descendant. These traditions already held the four rules: the ratio, women's magic, the rarity of fertile men and the power of pregnancy. What they lacked was number and test, not observation.

question.ask: What does the seven petals rhyme count?

topics.title: The Early Natural Philosophers
topics.content: Natural philosophy began when the rules were counted instead of recited. Birth rolls kept by the Order gave the first firm figures and showed the ratio to be the same in famine and plenty, in city and on farm. Early philosophers argued over whether the Bloom was a goddess, a fluid or a habit of nature. The view that prevailed, and that Breedhaven still teaches, is that the Bloom is an active force in soil, water and blood and not a distant god.

question.ask: Whose birth rolls gave the first firm figures on the ratio?

topics.title: The Household and the Old Law
topics.content: With fertile men so few, the earliest law codes of the lowlands were household law. They fixed who belonged to a household, who inherited from it and what a fertile man owed the women who kept him. In the worst periods Sires were held, traded and fought over like land. The long reform of that practice, from possession to protection, is the main thread of Expanse legal history, and it is why paternity and reproductive contracts still have courts of their own.

question.ask: What kind of law were the earliest law codes of the lowlands?

topics.title: Dawnbloom, Seedblossom and the University
topics.content: Breedhaven took its lasting shape under House Dawnbloom, which bound the river lowlands and their orchards into one kingdom with its seat at Seedblossom. The University's oldest stone was laid some seven centuries ago on the north bank. By long custom the heir to the throne studies there, in what is now the College of Government and Law, among ordinary students. Notes between the colleges were once carried by runners, remembered today in the word courier.

question.ask: Which house bound the river lowlands into one kingdom?

topics.title: The Damper and the Freewill Movement
topics.content: For most of history a woman met the pull with nothing but her own resolve. The reliable suppressant changed that. Once dampers became cheap and ordinary, a woman could turn the pull down to a background hum and plan her years around something other than bearing. The modern Freewill movement grew from that experience, holding that the Bloom may influence a woman but does not own her. Bloomism took its modern form in reply, defending the pull as sacred.

question.ask: Which invention did the modern Freewill movement grow from?

topics.title: The Bloom and the Modern States
topics.content: Each modern state of the Expanse is an answer to the Bloom. Iscara gave rule to its strongest mages and built the long-range portal network. Kharad-Tor organized its holds under War-Mothers and a governing council. Veyra made coalition a principle. The Vesperan League began when pirate queens agreed to share the sea lanes. Breedhaven chose a crown checked by an elected Assembly, and a Sire Registry that both protects fertile men and keeps a file on them.

question.ask: What checks the power of the crown in Breedhaven?

skill.name: Habit of reading
skill.description: You read in every spare hour: Focus earns three quarters of a session, not half.

courses.title: Music Theory and Practice
courses.description: Foundations of melody, harmony, rhythm, and form, with an introduction to resonant and thaumically enhanced instruments. Weekly laboratory includes ensemble performance and ear training. No prerequisites.

topics.title: Pitch, Scale and the Octave
topics.content: Pitch is how high or low a note sounds. Doubling the speed of vibration gives the same note an octave higher, and the octave is divided into twelve equal semitones. A major scale picks seven of them in the pattern tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone. An old nursery rhyme calls the seven notes the seven sisters and the eighth, the octave, the brother who comes home. Sung up from C on the white keys of a piano, the scale needs no sharps or flats, which is why teaching starts there.

question.ask: From which note is a major scale sung on the white keys alone?

topics.title: Rhythm, Meter and Pulse
topics.content: Pulse is the steady beat under a piece; meter groups the beats into bars. Four beats to a bar is the commonest meter and the one Kharadi marching drums keep. Three to a bar is the waltz. Breedhaven's orchard work songs swing in six, two big beats each split in three, timed to the reach and drop of picking. Veyran dances often run in seven, counted two, two, three. A reliable exercise is to clap the pulse while speaking the rhythm, then to swap, until the two no longer pull each other off.

question.ask: How many beats to a bar do Breedhaven's orchard work songs have?

topics.title: Intervals, Chords and Harmony
topics.content: An interval is the distance between two notes. A triad stacks two thirds: C, E and G make the chord of C major. Three chords, built on the first, fourth and fifth notes of the scale, will harmonize most folk tunes, and the move from the fifth back to the first is the cadence that sounds like an ending. Because most singers are women, Breedhaven choral music is written for two soprano and two alto parts. A bass line, when a choir has the men for it, is called the ground and is a prized color.

question.ask: What is a bass line called in Breedhaven choral music?

topics.title: Resonant and Enhanced Instruments
topics.content: A resonant instrument has a charm built into its body, so a note rings longer and carries further: the resonant harp of the lowlands sustains a plucked string for ten seconds or more. A thaumically enhanced instrument is different: the player feeds it her own magic as she plays, bending tone and volume at will. It is tiring, and a pregnant player can overdrive one badly enough to crack it. Conservatoire auditions are played on plain instruments, so that the hands are what is judged.

question.ask: On what kind of instrument are conservatoire auditions played?

topics.title: Song Forms and Musical Structure
topics.content: Form is the plan of a piece. Binary form has two sections, A then B, each usually repeated. Ternary form returns home: A, B, A. Most popular songs alternate verse and chorus, the verse changing its words and the chorus keeping them. A round is one tune sung by several voices entering in turn, each starting when the last reaches the second line. Breedhaven lullabies are nearly all rounds, written so that every adult of a household can join one after another without waking the child.

question.ask: What form do nearly all Breedhaven lullabies take?

topics.title: Ensemble Playing and Ear Training
topics.content: An ensemble tunes to one A, given by the oboe, and every player then listens more than she plays. The first rule is to match the note's start and its end, not only its pitch. Ear training fixes each interval to a known tune: a rising fourth opens most marching songs, a rising fifth most hymns of the Order. Players sit in an arc so each can see the leader's breath. A choir that sings in a closed ring can carry a working as a circle does, which is why the Order's cathedral choirs stand in one.

question.ask: Which instrument gives the A that an ensemble tunes to?

skill.name: Ear for a mood
skill.description: You know how to set one: desire grows a quarter faster.

courses.title: Rhetoric and Debate
courses.description: Principles of argumentation, persuasion, and public speaking. Students analyze and construct arguments on topics of public controversy, including Bloom policy, Sire regulation, and royal prerogative. No prerequisites.

topics.title: Claim, Grounds and Warrant
topics.content: An argument has three working parts. The claim is what the speaker wants accepted. The grounds are the evidence offered. The warrant is the unstated rule linking the two, and it is where most arguments fail. Example: suppressants should stay free at clinics (claim), because uptake falls when a charge is made (grounds). The hidden warrant is that high uptake is good, which a Bloomist opponent may deny. Find the warrant, state it aloud, and the real disagreement appears.

question.ask: What is the unstated rule linking an argument's claim to its grounds called?

topics.title: Ethos, Pathos and Logos
topics.content: Persuasion works by three appeals. Ethos is the speaker's credibility: a midwife on Bloom Chambers is heard differently from a minister. Pathos is the audience's feeling, and logos is the reasoning itself. A speech that leans on one alone is weak. In the Assembly, a member arguing for Registry reform typically opens with standing, such as a Sire in her own household, moves to a single case that stirs the chamber, and only then gives numbers. Reverse the order and nobody listens long enough.

question.ask: Which of the three appeals rests on the speaker's credibility?

topics.title: Fallacies Common in Bloom Debates
topics.content: Four errors dominate public argument. The appeal to nature: the Bloom wants it, therefore it is right. The false dilemma: either the state tracks Sires or the nation dies out. The slippery slope: a Registry today, breeding quotas tomorrow, with no step shown between. And the argument against the person, in two local forms: she is on dampers, so she cannot feel what she is talking about, or she is pregnant, so that is the Bloom talking. Each attacks a speaker and leaves her case standing.

question.ask: Which fallacy argues that the Bloom wants it, so it is right?

topics.title: Motions, Rebuttal and Points of Information
topics.content: Formal debate follows Assembly practice. A motion is put, for instance that this house would let a Sire's household see his Registry record. Proposition and opposition field three speakers each, speaking alternately for seven minutes. First speakers define and build, second speakers rebut and extend, and third speakers weigh the clash without adding new matter. An opponent may rise to offer a point of information of fifteen seconds, which the speaker may accept or decline.

question.ask: How long does each speaker speak in a formal debate?

topics.title: Arguing the Royal Prerogative
topics.content: Any dispute can be sorted by four questions asked in order: what happened, what to call it, whether it was justified, and what should be done. Take a monarch who withholds assent from a bill, which has not occurred in over a century. Fact: was assent refused or only delayed? Definition: is that a lawful use of prerogative or a breach of convention? Quality: did circumstances excuse it? Policy: should assent be made automatic by statute? Most debaters lose by answering the fourth question first.

question.ask: Most debaters lose by answering which of the four questions first?

topics.title: Delivery, Audience and the Fair Close
topics.content: Delivery is pace, pause and eye. A trained speaker runs near 150 words a minute and slows for whatever she most wants remembered. Audience comes next. Seven in eight listeners are women, and a speech on Sire regulation that speaks of men as though none were in the room loses the men and the fair-minded with them. The strongest close concedes something true to the other side before restating the claim. A concession costs a speaker one point and buys her credit on every other.

question.ask: What does the strongest close do before restating the claim?
question.answer: Concedes something true to the other side
